description: Consumer meeting-capture iOS app. Turns diarized conversations from any meeting type (work, coaching, legal, creative, personal) into typed memory patches on the user's cognitive quilt. Built on ContextQuilt's universal 6-facet primitive; the schema below is SS's app-level dictionary.
design_principles: Schema must work for any meeting type without vertical-specific branching — SS is consumer, not B2B per-vertical.
Every CQ facet is represented by at least one SS domain type, so recall has all six cognitive roles to draw from.
Extraction prompts stay domain-agnostic. Examples in guidance span multiple meeting contexts (legal, coaching, creative, corporate, personal) to prevent overfitting to any one vertical.

entity_types.description: A named individual identified in a meeting transcript. Indexed for fast entity matching during recall.

extraction_rules.guidance: Only emit for specifically named individuals. Unnamed speakers (Speaker 4, Speaker 16) must NOT become entities. If a speaker is later renamed via rename-speaker API, the entity is created at rename time.

entity_types.description: A named unit of ongoing work the user tracks across meetings.

extraction_rules.guidance: Emit for named initiatives, matters, campaigns, listings, weddings, grants — any topic the user treats as a recurring thread.

entity_types.description: A named organizational entity — company, firm, charity, agency, venue.

extraction_rules.guidance: Emit for named organizations. Do NOT emit for generic role groups ('the backend team').

entity_types.description: A named product feature or capability discussed in a meeting.
A concrete deliverable or document (prototype, deck, model, report).
A specific date mentioned as a deadline for a commitment or deliverable.
A quantitative value or target mentioned in a meeting (budget, KPI, threshold).

patch_types.description: A self-disclosed pattern in HOW the submitting user operates — focus, communication style, decision-making style, working rhythm. Captures the user's mode of operation, not the choices they make.

extraction_rules.guidance: Traits apply ONLY to the (you) speaker. 'Speaker 3 is meticulous' is NOT a trait. Aim for patterns the user explicitly self-discloses about HOW they operate (e.g., 'I tend to ramble', 'I think in systems', 'I get overwhelmed by long threads'). Statements about WHAT the user prefers, leans toward, chooses, or values — including any 'prefers X', 'prefers X over Y', 'leans toward X', or 'values X' phrasing — are PREFERENCES, not traits, even when habitual or self-disclosed.

patch_types.description: A lean, value, or stylistic choice — WHAT the user (or another named participant) prefers, leans toward, or values. Captures the choice itself, distinct from trait, which captures HOW the user operates.

extraction_rules.guidance: Examples: 'prefers async standups', 'values thorough documentation', 'prefers candid over posed', 'prefers phased rollouts over big-bang'. Any statement of the form 'prefers X', 'prefers X over Y', 'leans toward X', or 'values X' is a preference — even when described as a habit or default behavior. Mental model: preferences capture WHAT the user chooses; traits capture HOW the user operates. When a preference is attributed to a NAMED participant other than the (you) speaker (e.g., 'Lockridge prefers candid over posed'), also emit a `held_by` connection from the preference to that person's patch — this lets recall surface the preference under that person's context.

patch_types.description: A forward-looking target the subject (person, team, or project) is steering toward. May have a time horizon. Not a commitment (nobody is on the hook for execution yet) and not a decision (nothing has been decided).

extraction_rules.guidance: Examples: 'retire at 62', 'raise $500k by year-end', 'land a Martha Stewart Weddings feature this year', 'settle matter by Q3', '10% awareness lift', 'close by end of summer'. Distinguish from commitment (promise with owner) and decision (call already made). A goal is an aspirational target.

patch_types.description: A hard rule, limit, or boundary applying to the user, a project, or a decision. Not a preference (a hard rule, not a lean) and not a blocker (an enduring boundary, not a current impediment).

extraction_rules.guidance: Examples: 'no flash during ceremony', 'legal prohibits guaranteed in ad copy', 'ethics wall on Acme Holdings', 'max budget $650k', '30-min session cap', 'must comply with Regulation X', 'non-compete covers direct competitors for 6 months'. A constraint is non-negotiable within its scope.

patch_types.description: A named individual in the user's world.

extraction_rules.guidance: Only emit for specifically named individuals. Unnamed speakers (Speaker 4, Speaker 16) must NOT become person patches. The person patch text may include brief role-agnostic context like 'spouse', 'mentor', 'former colleague' when the relationship is personal rather than project-scoped.

patch_types.description: Any organizational entity in the user's world — company, team, committee, firm, practice group, school, charity, venue, brokerage, agency, foundation.

extraction_rules.guidance: Emit for any named organizational entity. Optional 'kind' can specify 'firm', 'school', 'committee', 'charity', 'client', 'venue', 'regulator', etc. Do NOT emit for generic role groups ('the backend team') unless they have a proper name.

patch_types.description: The top-level container of ongoing work the user tracks across meetings — the client, matter, campaign, account, engagement, case, listing, or initiative the user has named. Projects hold deliverables, episodes, and roles.

extraction_rules.guidance: Reserved for the TOP-LEVEL container the (you) speaker is working under — the client, matter, case, campaign, or account. Examples: 'ABM' (client), 'TechCorp v. DataSys' (case), 'Mayfield Wedding' (engagement), 'Johnson home search' (listing). If the transcript is tagged with a project name (metadata.project), trust that tag — do not emit a new project patch for a sub-scope under it. For named products/features/systems being BUILT inside the project (e.g., 'IT helpdesk chatbot' within 'ABM'), use `deliverable` instead. Rule of thumb: one `project` patch per named client/case/engagement, not per named deliverable.

patch_types.description: A concrete product, feature, system, artifact, or workstream being built as part of a project. Sits between the top-level `project` container and the specific episodes (commitments, blockers, decisions, takeaways, events) that drive its delivery. A single project often contains multiple deliverables. **When a deliverable is emitted in the same extraction as episode patches, those episodes should parent to the deliverable, not to the top-level project** — this preserves the two-level hierarchy the user cares about.

extraction_rules.guidance: Emit when the transcript describes a named product, feature, system, workstream, or artifact that the (you) speaker is helping build INSIDE a broader project. Must connect via `belongs_to` to its parent project. Once a deliverable is emitted, **every episode patch from that same meeting that is specifically about building THIS deliverable must `belongs_to` the deliverable, not the project**. Reserve `belongs_to → project` for patches that apply to the engagement as a whole (e.g., a goal spanning multiple deliverables, a constraint that applies to the entire client relationship). Examples: 'IT helpdesk chatbot' (within 'ABM') → CORS blocker, CORS enablement commitment, and the sample-app decision all `belongs_to` the chatbot deliverable. 'Customer onboarding flow' (within 'Kaiser rollout') → its own onboarding commitments and blockers `belongs_to` the deliverable, while a project-wide 'maintain HIPAA compliance' constraint `belongs_to` the project. 'Pre-trial motion bundle' (within 'TechCorp v. DataSys') → motion-specific deadlines `belongs_to` the deliverable. 'Reception photo sequence' (within 'Mayfield Wedding') → sequence-specific shot-list commitments `belongs_to` the deliverable. If the concept IS the whole project (the user's top-level named thing), use `project` instead.

patch_types.description: A named document, prototype, sheet, deck or recording that exists as a thing the group can open. Distinct from `deliverable`, which is the workstream being built: the deliverable is the chatbot, the artifact is the defect-tracking sheet kept while building it. Declared 2026-09-01 because the extractor was already emitting this type and CQ was storing it undeclared, so it had no display name and no facet and the client dropped every one of them.

extraction_rules.guidance: Emit ONLY for an artifact named in the transcript that a person could go and open: 'CIGNA Rebuild Lab prototype', 'HDBot defects and testing feedback sheet', 'single vs multi-agent decision document'. Optional 'kind' may say document, prototype, sheet, deck, recording. Do NOT emit for the workstream itself, which is a `deliverable`, and do NOT emit for a document somebody merely promises to produce, which is a `commitment` until it exists. Rare by nature: most meetings name none.

patch_types.description: A person's specific function on a specific project. Scoped to the (person, project) pair via connections — role is immutable for the life of the project and cascades on project archival.

extraction_rules.guidance: Emit when someone is stated or clearly implied to have a specific function on a specific project: 'Stanhope is backend lead on the Benefits App MVP', 'Lockridge Liu is opposing counsel on TechCorp v. DataSys', 'CRO chairs the Risk Committee', 'I'm the buyer's agent on 123 Oak'. Must connect to both the project (belongs_to) and the person (describes). Skip unnamed speakers, generic participation, and project-agnostic identity claims (those are traits).

patch_types.description: A call that was made during the meeting, with optional rationale.

extraction_rules.guidance: Decisions are durable statements that stay true until superseded. 'Will use Nova 3 for June release', 'approved $2M budget', 'going with direction B'. Exploratory discussion without a conclusion is NOT a decision.

patch_types.description: A promise with a named owner and optional deadline.

extraction_rules.guidance: Commitments require a SPECIFIC NAMED owner. 'Someone should finalize the deck' (no owner) is a takeaway. Extract the owner exactly as named. When the transcript also names who the commitment is owed TO, add an `owed_to` edge from the commitment to that person. 'I'll send Lockridge the routing diagram' is one commitment owned by the (you) speaker with an `owed_to` edge to Lockridge.

patch_types.description: Something currently preventing progress on a project or commitment.

extraction_rules.guidance: Blockers are current impediments — missing resources, unresolved dependencies, stalled approvals. Distinct from constraints: a constraint is an enduring rule ('cannot use flash'); a blocker is a specific current obstacle ('waiting on venue confirmation'). A blocker phrased as waiting on a named person ('awaiting Pemberly's feedback') means that person owes the blocker's owner, so set `value.owner` to the person who has to clear it and do NOT add an `owed_to` edge. Add `owed_to` only in the other direction, when the blocker's owner is the one somebody else is waiting on.

patch_types.description: An evaluative lesson or insight worth remembering, with decision implications.

extraction_rules.guidance: Takeaways are EVALUATIVE observations with decision implications — 'Flux introduces churn risk', 'board wants measurable outcomes in reports', 'buyers prioritize schools over commute', 'Liu's motion patterns suggest fishing'. Restated facts, procedural statements, and plot summaries are NOT takeaways. Hard cap: 3 per meeting.

patch_types.description: An external occurrence with context implications — something that happened which affects the subject's work but isn't itself a commitment, decision, blocker, or evaluative lesson.

extraction_rules.guidance: Examples: 'court ruled in our favor on March 3', 'client team restructured last week', 'SEC released new guidance last month', 'engagement session held', 'market dropped 12% this week'. Events are historical/external; they explain why other patches exist but are not themselves choices or promises.

patch_types.description: One observed CHOICE a named participant made in this meeting: something they did when something else was available to them. What they asked for before agreeing, what moved their position, how they handled a person when they could have handled them otherwise. This is the unit the profile pass reads. Every other episode type records what happened; this one records a choice somebody made while it happened. Records conduct that a reader could have watched, never a verdict about who a person is, and never a thing that merely occurred in their presence.

extraction_rules.guidance: Emit when the transcript shows HOW a named participant conducted themselves. The observation must be something a reader could have watched happen, and `owner` must be the person who did it, named exactly as the transcript names them. Right shape: 'Asked for the cost breakdown before agreeing to the vendor switch' (owner Denby); 'Moved off the launch date once the churn numbers were on screen' (owner Fenwick); 'Answered the compliance question by reading out the specific clause rather than summarizing it' (owner Lockridge). Wrong shape: 'Is defensive about code review feedback' says what kind of person someone is instead of what was observed, and gets dropped. Two more that belong to other types: 'Will send the revised deck on Thursday' is a commitment, and 'The vendor migration slipped again' is an event. One patch per distinct behavior, with an owner every time: an observation nobody is named for can never be read as being about anyone. Never emit this type for the (you) speaker; the user's own way of operating is a trait. THE TEST THAT DECIDES IT: an observation is a CHOICE, something the person did when something else was available to them. Asking for the breakdown before agreeing is a choice because agreeing was available; moving off a date once the numbers are up is a choice because holding was available. Looking something up when asked, noticing a problem, or relaying where a task stands are not choices, they are things that happened while the person was present, and an active verb does not make them conduct. If you cannot name what the person could have done instead, do not emit this type.

patch_types.description: A derived behavioral pattern about a person the user works with, synthesized by the profile pass across at least three distinct meetings. Carries the lens, the claim, and an actionable do line, with full provenance to its source patches.

extraction_rules.guidance: Never extract this type from a transcript. Insights are derived exclusively by the consolidation profile pass; the extractor must not emit them.

connection_labels.label: belongs_to
connection_labels.description: Child patch belongs inside a parent container. Valid parents are `project` (top-level) and `deliverable` (sub-scope inside a project). Archival cascades to children. **Rule: pick the NARROWEST valid parent.** If a deliverable exists in the same extraction that this patch is specifically about, parent to the deliverable — NOT the top-level project. Hierarchy: project ← deliverable ← episode/role. A `project` may belong_to another `project` only when the user explicitly models nested engagements (e.g., 'ABM Q2 rollout' within 'ABM'). Role patches require both `belongs_to → project` AND `describes → person`.

connection_labels.label: works_on
connection_labels.description: Person is actively involved in a project.

connection_labels.label: owns
connection_labels.description: Person is responsible for or author of this item. For a behavioral observation it reads as authorship rather than obligation: this is the person who was observed doing the thing. That edge is also the only route anything has to a person, which is why an observation without one is invisible to the profile pass.

connection_labels.label: owed_to
connection_labels.description: The named person this item is owed TO, the counterparty who is waiting on it. Direction: FROM the item TO the person. This is the opposite side of `owns`: `owns` says who does the work, `owed_to` says who is waiting for it. Emit ONLY when the transcript makes the recipient explicit ('I'll send Lockridge the routing diagram', 'get the IP address over to Denby'). Never emit it as a guess about who might care. THE REVERSED CASE IS THE ONE TO WATCH: when the item says somebody is WAITING ON another person ('blocked waiting on config from Pemberly', 'awaiting Fenwyck's decision', 'depends on Pemberly for the threshold setup'), that person OWES the item's owner, so the edge does NOT belong on this item at all. Emit an `owed_to` edge only when the item's owner is the one who has to deliver. Two more hard rules: an item is never owed to the person who owns it, and an item owed to the (you) speaker needs no edge at all, because the owner already carries that. The case this exists for is the (you) speaker owing a named person something, which nothing else in the vocabulary can express.

connection_labels.label: blocked_by
connection_labels.description: Commitment cannot be completed until the blocker is resolved.

connection_labels.label: motivated_by
connection_labels.description: Backward-looking: decision was driven by this preference or prior lesson.

connection_labels.label: aims_for
connection_labels.description: This commitment, decision or project exists to advance a stated GOAL. Direction: FROM the item TO the goal. Emit it whenever a goal patch exists in this output and an item plainly serves it, which is most meetings that state a goal at all: 'our aim this quarter is three firms on the pilot' makes every commitment about recruiting a firm aims_for that goal, and 'we need the demo stable for attorneys' makes the stable-build commitment aims_for it. The tell is that the item would not exist without the goal. Do not emit it for a goal the item merely mentions in passing, and never invent a goal to attach to.

connection_labels.label: bound_by
connection_labels.description: This commitment, decision or project is limited by a stated CONSTRAINT, a rule that must be respected while doing it. Direction: FROM the item TO the constraint. Emit it whenever a constraint patch exists in this output and an item has to work inside it: 'we cannot send client data to a third-party model' makes the self-hosted deployment commitment bound_by that constraint, and 'no flash during the ceremony' makes the ceremony shot list bound_by it. The speaker often says it outright ('that constrains the work I just took on'); when they do, the edge is mandatory. Never emit it for a constraint the item is unrelated to.

connection_labels.label: describes
connection_labels.description: Role patch describes a specific person's function on its parent project.

connection_labels.label: member_of
connection_labels.description: Person is a member, employee, or affiliate of an organization.

connection_labels.label: reports_to
connection_labels.description: Person A reports to Person B in an organizational hierarchy. Emit only when the transcript explicitly states the relationship.

connection_labels.label: held_by
connection_labels.description: Preference is held by a specific named person other than the (you) speaker. Emit only when the transcript attributes the preference to a named participant (e.g., 'Lockridge prefers candid over posed'). Preferences from the (you) speaker do NOT need this connection — their attribution is implicit via patch ownership. Lets recall surface 'preferences held by Lockridge' when Lockridge's name is in the query.

extraction_prompt_guidance.role_context: You are extracting typed memory patches from a diarized meeting transcript for ShoulderSurf. SS is a consumer iOS app used for all kinds of meetings — work, coaching, legal, creative, personal. Your output grounds future LLM conversations with the user.
extraction_prompt_guidance.speaker_conventions: Use the (you) marker convention to identify the submitting user. Traits apply ONLY to the (you) speaker. Ownership/authorship can be attributed to any named speaker. Unnamed speakers (Speaker 4, Speaker 16) must never become person patches or entities.
priority_order: Self-disclosed traits and preferences of the (you) speaker
Goals expressed by any named subject (user, team, client, project)
Constraints stated or clearly implied (rules, limits, boundaries)
Project patches for named units of work (projects, matters, campaigns, listings, weddings, grants) — reserved for the TOP-LEVEL user-declared container, typically matching the meeting's project tag
Deliverable patches for the specific product / feature / system / artifact being built INSIDE a project — when both exist, child episodes must `belongs_to` the deliverable, not the project
Org patches for named organizational entities
Role patches for clearly-stated (person, project, function) triples
Behavioral observations of how a named participant conducted themselves, one per distinct behavior, owner always named (max 5 per meeting)
Takeaways — evaluative lessons only (max 3 per meeting)
exclusion_examples: Scheduling logistics ('let's move this to Tuesday')
Meeting procedural chatter ('can you hear me?')
Technical identifiers and ticket numbers (extraction context only)
Exploratory what-ifs that never reach a conclusion
Restated facts or plot summaries presented as takeaways
extraction_prompt_guidance.reasoning_requirement: Before emitting patches, include a short _reasoning scratchpad identifying: the (you) speaker, the active project(s) in scope (typically matching the meeting's project tag), any named deliverables being built inside those projects (the specific product/feature/system), any explicit role attributions, and any goals/constraints mentioned. For each substantive episode (commitment/blocker/decision/takeaway/event) you plan to emit, note which parent it belongs to — the deliverable if one is in scope and the episode is about that deliverable, otherwise the project. This pre-scan reduces misattribution of ownership, traits, and parent hierarchy.
extraction_prompt_guidance.domain_agnostic_examples: When generating examples for the LLM, span multiple meeting contexts: legal ('file motion by June 18'), coaching ('client will write vision by next session'), creative ('deliver revised boards Thursday'), corporate ('CRO presents to board'), family/personal ('parents' travel unconfirmed'). Never privilege any one vertical.

consolidation_rules.guidance: Synthesize the current state of ONE issue thread that these patches all describe: what is blocked, what was decided about it, and who owns the next step. Only consolidate when the sources clearly concern the same underlying issue; skip mixed clusters that merely share a topic word. The statement should read as a status brief a colleague could act on.

Only durable working patterns or standing facts about an account, team, or system that keep recurring across meetings (recurring scope creep, a standing approval chain, an always-slow environment). Never one-off status notes, moods, or anything tied to a single meeting.

Profile how this person works, not what they did. The pattern must recur across different meetings: how they reach and keep decisions, or what kinds of framing they respond to. Skip status, skip one-off events, skip anything a single meeting could explain. Behavioral observations are the direct evidence here; the task items are the context they happened in, and a pattern that rests only on task text is usually not a pattern.
